summary: This unit teaches you to clean a villa or small hotel kitchen so that food stays safe: the difference between cleaning, disinfecting and sanitising, the stages of a proper clean, how to use cleaning chemicals safely, how to follow a cleaning schedule, how to clean equipment, wash up by hand, clean floors and drains, handle waste and oil, and spot and report pests.

blocks.p: A kitchen can look clean and still carry germs. Cleaning is not only about appearance: it removes the dirt, grease and food scraps that germs and pests live on, and it makes sure that the next meal is not spoilt by the last one. This unit is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees. Every cook and kitchen assistant cleans, so it is a skill you will use every day of your working life.

Cleaning chemicals, hot water, sharp blades and electrical equipment can all hurt you. That is why this unit is about **safe methods** as much as clean results: you must know what a product is, how strong to make it, what to wear, and what never to mix.

The assessor watches how you work as well as how clean the result is.

sections.title: Cleaning words and the stages of cleaning

blocks.h: Why a kitchen must be cleaned

ul: To remove dirt, grease and food waste that feed bacteria, flies and rats.
To stop germs passing from one food to another (cross-contamination).
To prevent slips, fires (from built-up grease) and breakdowns of equipment.
To meet the law and the standards that public health inspectors check.
To protect guests, staff and the business's name.

blocks.h: Four words that are often mixed up

head: Word
What it means
Kitchen example
rows: Cleaning
Removing dirt, grease and food waste, usually with detergent and water. It does not kill all germs, but dirt must go first.
Washing a pot in hot, soapy water.
Disinfecting
Using a chemical (or very hot water) to reduce germs on a clean surface. Disinfectants may be stronger than sanitisers.
Wiping a clean board with disinfectant, then leaving it for the contact time.
Sanitising

Reducing germs on a clean surface to a safe level for food. A food-safe sanitiser is used on food-contact surfaces. Some products combine a detergent and a sanitiser in one, but they still work best on a surface that is already visibly clean.
Spraying a food-safe sanitiser on a washed chopping board.
Sterilising
Killing all germs, including spores, for example with steam under pressure (autoclave). It is not normally done in a kitchen.
Hospitals sterilise surgical tools.

blocks.note: Dirt and grease protect germs and use up the chemical, so a disinfectant or sanitiser does not work well on a dirty surface. **Always clean first, then disinfect or sanitise.**
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: The stages of cleaning a surface or a piece of equipment

flow: Make it safe: switch off and unplug electrical items; let hot items cool
Pre-clean: scrape or wipe loose food and waste into the bin
Main clean: wash with hot water and detergent, using a cloth or brush
Rinse with clean water to remove the detergent and loosened dirt
Disinfect or sanitise with a food-safe product at the right strength, for the full contact time
Final rinse with clean water, if the label says
Dry: let it air-dry, or use a clean disposable cloth

blocks.p: Many kitchens call these the **six stages of cleaning**: pre-clean, main clean, rinse, disinfect, final rinse and dry. A two-stage method, **clean then disinfect**, is the shorter way of saying the same thing. Follow the method that the Centre's cleaning schedule gives.

Hot water helps to dissolve grease and loosen dirt, but wash water for hand-washing is limited by what your gloved hands can stand, usually about 45 to 50 °C. Chemical sanitisers are often used at room temperature or warm, as the label says. Some kitchens sanitise by dipping items in very hot water (about 77 °C or hotter, for about 30 seconds) or by a dishwasher final rinse of 80 °C or more. These figures vary by maker and by the Centre's plan; follow your instructor.

blocks.note: Water in much of Jamaica is hard and leaves white scale on kettles, steamers, taps and dishwashers. A descaler removes it, and a rinse aid helps dishes dry without spots.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Cleaning chemicals do their work because they are strong, which means they can also burn skin, harm eyes and lungs, and make food unsafe. Use only the chemicals the Centre supplies for the job, and only after you have been shown how.

head: Product
What it is for
Take care
rows: Detergent (washing-up liquid, cleaning detergent)
Lifts dirt and grease from surfaces and dishes.
Does not kill germs on its own.
Degreaser
Strong detergent for heavy grease: cooker hoods, filters, grills, extractor fans.
Stronger and can burn skin: gloves and eye protection.
Disinfectant
Reduces germs on clean surfaces such as toilets and floors, as the label says.
Check that it is safe for food-contact surfaces before using it on those.
Food-safe sanitiser
Reduces germs on clean food-contact surfaces: boards, benches, knives, utensils.
Use at the strength on the label. Some need rinsing; some are no-rinse.
Descaler (acid)
Removes lime scale from kettles, steamers, dishwashers and taps.
Acid. Never mix with bleach. Rinse well afterwards.
Oven cleaner
Removes baked-on carbon and grease.
Very caustic. Gloves, eye protection and good air flow.
Abrasive (scouring) cleaner or pad
Fine grit that scrubs off burnt-on food.
Can scratch stainless steel, plastic and non-stick, and the scratches trap dirt.
Bleach (hypochlorite)
A strong disinfectant for some surfaces.
Gives off poisonous chlorine gas if mixed with acids or ammonia products.

blocks.h: Read the label and the SDS

blocks.p: The **label** on the container tells you what the product is, how to dilute and use it, how long to leave it on, and the main warnings. The **safety data sheet (SDS)** is a longer sheet from the maker that gives the dangers, the PPE to wear, how to store it, what to do in a spill or fire and the **first aid**. Your workplace must keep an SDS for each chemical where staff can find it. Read both **before** you open a new product.

Most concentrates must be diluted with water. The label gives a ratio such as 'X ml per litre of water'. Measure with a jug or a dispenser; do not guess. Too weak and it will not clean or kill germs. Too strong and it can burn skin, damage surfaces, leave residue on food-contact surfaces and waste money.

head: Label says
You need
Working
Answer
rows: 25 ml per litre
8 litres of solution
200 ml of concentrate in 8 litres of water (add to the water to make the total volume 8 litres)
50 ml per litre
5 litres of solution
250 ml in 5 litres of water
1 part concentrate to 20 parts water
A 500 ml spray bottle (almost full)
500 ÷ 21 is about 24
About 25 ml of concentrate; top up with water to 500 ml

blocks.p: **Add the chemical to the water, not the water to the chemical**, to avoid splashing the strong concentrate. Use cold or warm water as the label says: very hot water can give off fumes from some chemicals.

A disinfectant or sanitiser needs time to kill germs. The **contact time** is the time that the surface must stay wet with the product, and it is printed on the label. If you wipe it off straight away, the germs are still alive.
**PPE** means **personal protective equipment**. The label and SDS say which to wear.

head: PPE
When
rows: Chemical-resistant gloves
Handling concentrates, oven cleaner, degreaser, descaler, bleach, and for hot water.
Eye protection (goggles or a visor)
Pouring concentrates, spraying overhead or where there is a splash risk.
Apron
Protects clothes and skin from splashes.
Non-slip, closed shoes
All cleaning, especially floors.
Cut-resistant glove
Cleaning near sharp blades, as part of the maker's method.
Mask or good ventilation
Strong fumes, if the SDS says so. Open windows or use the extractor fan.

blocks.note: Never mix cleaning products. **Bleach mixed with an acid cleaner (a descaler or toilet cleaner) gives off chlorine, a poisonous, choking gas. Bleach mixed with ammonia gives off other toxic fumes.** If you smell a sharp, choking gas, leave at once, get into fresh air and warn others. Do not try to clear it up yourself. Tell your supervisor. Rinse a bucket well before it is used for another product.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Keep chemicals in a locked or separate cupboard or room, away from food, clean dishes and packaging, with the SDS to hand.
Keep them in their **original labelled containers**. Never put cleaner in a drink bottle or food container: someone could drink it.
If you fill a spray bottle from a concentrate, label it with the name of the product, the dilution and the date, and the hazard symbol.
Store heavy containers on low shelves. Keep lids tight. Do not store near heat.
Report leaking, damaged or unlabelled containers.

head: Accident
First action
rows: Splash in the eye
Hold the eye open under gently running clean water straight away, for at least 10 to 15 minutes (follow the SDS), then get medical help.
Splash on the skin
Remove contaminated clothes and wash the skin with plenty of water. Get help if it burns or blisters.
Swallowed
Do not make the person vomit. Rinse the mouth, and get medical help straight away, taking the container or SDS.
Fumes breathed in
Get into fresh air; get medical help if there is coughing, difficulty breathing or chest pain.
Spill on the floor
Put out a wet-floor sign. Use the spill method on the SDS. Wear PPE. Never wash strong chemicals down the sink without reading the SDS.

blocks.p: In every case, tell your supervisor and record the accident in the accident book.

sections.title: The cleaning schedule and kitchen routines

blocks.p: **Clean as you go** means cleaning spills, boards and tools while you work, not leaving everything until the end. It keeps the bench clear, stops food and dirt drying hard, prevents slips and cross-contamination, and makes the final clean much shorter.
A **cleaning schedule** is a written plan, often a chart on the kitchen wall, of everything that must be cleaned. For each item or area it shows:

ul: **What** is to be cleaned (for example benches, boards, stove, fridges, floor, drains, hood filters, bins);
**When** or how often (after each use, daily, weekly, monthly);
**How** (the method and the stages);
**With what** (the chemical, the dilution, the cloth or brush);
**Who** is responsible, and a place to **sign and date** when it is done;
**Checked by** the supervisor.

blocks.p: Staff sign the schedule so that the supervisor and the inspector can see that the task was done, and by whom. If a task is missed, the schedule shows it, and it can be put right. A signed schedule that is not true is a serious matter: never sign for something you have not done.

head: How often
Typical tasks
rows: After every use
Boards, knives, utensils, the bench you worked on, spills, the slicer or mixer you used, hand-wash basin.
Daily, at the end of service
All benches, stove top, griddle, sinks, floors and drains, bins emptied and washed, fridge doors and handles, wipe-down of equipment, dishwasher emptied and cleaned.
Weekly
Inside of fridges and freezers, hood filters (or more often in busy kitchens), shelves, walls near the stove, the grease trap if the schedule says.
Monthly or on a set date
Deep clean: move equipment and clean behind and under it, descale the kettle and dishwasher, clean the extractor hood and fan, check and clean door seals, wash walls and ceiling.

blocks.p: Colour codes stop germs moving from dirty areas to clean ones. One common code is: red for toilets and bathroom floors, blue for the kitchen (general), green for food-preparation areas and food-contact surfaces, yellow for general areas and hand-wash basins, and so on. Codes differ between workplaces, so learn the one at your Centre.

ul: Never use a toilet mop or cloth in the kitchen, or a kitchen cloth in the toilet.
Change cloths often, or use disposable cloths or paper towels: a dirty or damp cloth spreads germs around.
Wash cloths and mop heads in hot water and disinfect them, then dry them. Do not leave a wet cloth in a pile.
If you use a bucket of sanitiser solution for wiping, make it fresh at the start of each shift and change it when it is dirty or after the time the plan says.
**Look**: no dirt, grease, streaks or crumbs.
**Feel**: surfaces are smooth, with no stickiness.
**Smell**: no sour smell or chemical smell left.
**Supervisor check**: signs the schedule.
Some businesses also use swab tests that measure hidden dirt, which show whether a surface that looks clean really is.

blocks.p: Always follow the maker's cleaning instructions and the Centre's rules. The notes here are general. **Before you clean any electrical item: switch off at the switch, unplug, and let it cool.**

ul: Clear the bench, scrape off waste, wash with detergent, rinse, sanitise with a food-safe sanitiser and let it air-dry.
Wooden boards are hard to clean and may be banned; many kitchens use plastic boards. Replace boards with deep cuts, because food and germs hide in them.
Scrub the sinks and taps, including the underside of the taps and the plug hole. Clean the hand-wash basin separately. It is for hands only.
Stainless steel: use a soft cloth or non-abrasive pad and wipe along the grain. Steel wool and harsh scourers scratch it, and the scratches trap dirt and germs.

ol: Wait until the equipment is switched off and cool enough to touch safely.
Take off removable parts (grids, burner caps, drip trays) and wash them in the sink.
Scrape off burnt food; apply degreaser or oven cleaner as the label says; leave it for the stated time.
Wipe off, rinse the surface well so no chemical is left, and dry.
Wipe the controls and knobs with a damp cloth. Do not spray cleaner into the controls or onto electrical parts, or into the gas ports.
Refit the parts and check that the burners light correctly.

blocks.note: Oven cleaner is very caustic. Wear gloves and eye protection, keep the area well ventilated, never use it on a hot surface, and rinse well. Do not use it on aluminium or non-stick surfaces unless the label allows.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: The hood and its filters trap grease from the air. If **grease builds up** in the filters and the duct, a spark or a flame flaring from a pan can set it alight, and a hood fire spreads fast. Clean the filters regularly, as the schedule says (often weekly, or more often in a busy kitchen).

ul: Switch off the fan; take out the filters carefully when the area is cool.
Soak or wash them in hot water with a degreaser, scrub, rinse and dry fully (or use the dishwasher if the maker allows).
Wipe the inside of the hood. Duct cleaning is done by a trained contractor.
Refit the filters the right way round and write it on the schedule.
Switch off and unplug, and wait until the oil has cooled enough to handle safely, as the maker's instructions say. Hot oil causes severe burns.
Drain the oil into a suitable container. Strain it if it is to be kept, or dispose of it if it is dark, foams or smells.
Clean the tank with hot water and a fryer cleaner or degreaser, scrub, rinse and dry. Water left in the fryer will make fresh oil spit.
Wipe the outside and the basket, refit the drain valve and close it before refilling.

flow: Plan the job for a quiet time
Move food into another fridge or a cool box with ice, and check the dates and labels. Throw away out-of-date, unlabelled or spoiled food
Switch off if the maker says
Take out the shelves and drawers and wash, rinse and sanitise them
Wash the inside walls, floor and door with detergent; rinse; sanitise; dry
Clean the door seal with a soft brush, paying attention to the folds, where mould grows. A torn seal must be reported
Switch on and let the fridge reach 5 °C or below before returning the food
Return the food in the right order, raw food at the bottom, and record the temperature

ol: Remove the bowl, blade or attachments carefully by their handles. Do not put your hand on a blade.
Wash the removable parts in the sink with hot water and detergent, rinse, sanitise and air-dry.
Wipe the motor base and body with a damp cloth. **Never put the motor base in water, hose it down or leave it to soak**: water in the motor causes a shock or a fire.
When the parts are dry, refit them and check that every guard and safety lid clicks into place. If a guard will not fit, do not use the machine and report it.

blocks.p: A slicer is one of the most dangerous machines in a kitchen. **Only a trained person may clean it**, following the maker's instructions. Switch it off at the switch and unplug it, then set the blade gap to zero so that the edge is covered. Wear a **cut-resistant glove** on the hand near the blade. Remove the parts the maker allows to be removed, wash, rinse and sanitise them, and wipe the blade with a cloth held so that your hand moves away from the cutting edge. Refit the guards before use.

blocks.h: Small equipment: can opener, microwave, kettle, toaster

ul: **Can opener:** take off the cutting wheel if it comes off, wash, sanitise and dry. Food dried on the blade can fall into the next tin.
**Microwave:** wipe the inside with a damp cloth and mild detergent; clean the door seal and the turntable. Steam from a bowl of water softens baked-on food.
**Kettle and steamer:** descale as the maker says, then boil and discard clean water more than once to remove the descaler.
**Toaster:** unplug, let it cool, empty the crumb tray and wipe the outside. Never poke a knife into it.

blocks.note: Jamaica's supply is 110 V, 50 Hz. Check that plugs and cables are not cracked or worn when you clean, and tell your supervisor if they are. Do not use the item until it has been repaired.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Washing up by hand and by machine

blocks.p: A **three-compartment sink** has one bowl for washing, one for rinsing and one for sanitising. If the kitchen has two bowls, wash in one and rinse and sanitise in the other, in turn.

flow: Clean and sanitise the sinks and draining boards first
Fill sink 1 with hot water and detergent, sink 2 with clean hot water, sink 3 with a food-safe sanitiser at the label strength (or very hot water as the Centre's method says)
Scrape all food waste into the bin; soak anything with burnt-on food in sink 1
Wash: start with the cleanest items (glasses, cutlery) and finish with the greasiest pots; scrub with a brush or non-abrasive pad
Rinse in sink 2
Sanitise in sink 3, leaving them for the contact time
Drain and **air-dry** on a rack
Store clean items covered and off the floor; empty and clean the sinks and wipe the draining boards

ul: Wear gloves for hot water and chemicals.
Change the water when it becomes cool, greasy or dirty. Cold, greasy water cannot clean, and a dirty sanitiser does not sanitise.
Wash **knives one at a time** and never leave them in a sink where you cannot see them. Wash them handle-up, pointing the blade away from your hand.
**Burnt-on food:** soak in hot detergent water, then scrub with a suitable scourer. Do not use steel wool or harsh scourers on non-stick, aluminium or stainless steel.
Do not use tea towels to dry washed items: damp cloths carry germs. Air-drying is cleaner.
Wash glasses and cups first in fresh water. Stack plates, bowls and pans so water can drain.
Scrape off food waste first. Do not put in items that the maker says are not dishwasher safe (for example, wooden items or some non-stick pans).
Load plates and bowls facing the spray, with nothing stacked inside another. Do not overload.
Check the detergent and rinse-aid supply, and that the wash and final rinse temperatures are right (many machines show them on a display; the final rinse is often 80 °C or above, as the maker says).
After the cycle, let items air-dry. Hot items dry fast, so do not dry them with a cloth.
At the end of the day, empty the filters and spray arms, clean the inside, leave the door open to air out and descale as the maker says.

blocks.note: Hot water scalds, so when you lift items from a hot rinse or the dishwasher, use gloves, and open the door away from your face to let steam escape.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Floors, drains, waste and used oil

flow: Put out wet-floor signs before you start
Move bins, mats and small equipment out of the way
Sweep first to remove loose food and rubbish, including under benches
Mop with the colour-coded kitchen mop and a bucket of floor detergent at the right dilution (change the water when it is dirty)
Work from the far corner towards the door and the drain, so that you do not walk on the clean floor
Rinse (or squeegee the water to the drain) and let it dry. Leave the signs out until the floor is dry
Wash the mop and bucket, disinfect, and store the mop head up to dry

ul: Wear non-slip shoes and gloves.
Use separate mops and buckets for the kitchen and for the toilets, so toilet germs do not reach food areas.
**Spills:** wipe up at once, especially oil and grease. Put out a sign and clean again with degreaser if needed.
A **squeegee** is a tool with a long handle and a rubber blade, used to push water towards the drain.

blocks.p: Fat poured down the sink cools and sets in the pipes and blocks the drain and the sewer. A **grease trap** is a small tank on the sink waste pipe that catches fat and food waste before the water goes into the drain. It must be emptied and cleaned regularly, as the schedule says, usually by a trained person or a contractor, and the waste is not tipped down the drain.

ul: Use sink strainers and empty them into the bin.
Scrape plates before washing; wipe greasy pans with paper first.
Floor drains: lift the cover, remove waste with a gloved hand or scoop, scrub with detergent, rinse and sanitise. Blocked or smelly drains should be reported.
Use bins with tight lids, lined with a bag. A foot pedal avoids touching the lid.
Do not overfill. Tie and remove bags at the end of every shift, or sooner when full; in Jamaica's heat, waste soon smells and draws flies.
Wash and disinfect bins regularly, and wash your hands after handling them.
Keep the outside waste area clean and covered, and away from the kitchen door. Rats, dogs and flies go for open skips.
Let it cool completely. Hot oil burns.
Strain into a clean, lidded, labelled container and store it away from food until it is collected by an approved collector or reused as the Centre decides.
**Never pour it down the sink or a drain**: it blocks pipes and harms the environment.

blocks.p: Separate glass bottles, cans, plastic bottles and cardboard into marked containers, and rinse them so they do not smell or attract pests. Plastic bottles and cardboard are collected by recyclers in many parts of Jamaica. Follow the villa's or Centre's arrangements.

Pests carry germs on their feet and bodies and in their droppings, damage food and packaging, and cost a business its good name. In Jamaica's warm climate, the main kitchen pests are **cockroaches (roaches), rats, mice, flies and ants**.

head: Pest
Signs
What attracts it
rows: Rats and mice
Droppings; chewed bags, boxes and wires; greasy smears along walls; nests and gnawed holes; scratching noises at night
Open food, spills and waste; gaps in walls and under doors; clutter and cardboard to hide in
Cockroaches
Live or dead insects, usually seen at night or when you move a heavy item; egg cases; a stale, oily smell; dark spots
Warmth, damp and food crumbs behind stoves and fridges, in drains and in cardboard
Flies
Seen on food, bins and waste; maggots in old waste
Uncovered food, overflowing bins and waste, open doors
Ants
Trails to sugar, syrup and sweet spills
Sweet or greasy spills and crumbs

ul: **Deny them food**: clean as you go, wipe up spills, wash bins, keep food covered, in sealed containers.
**Deny them water**: fix leaks, dry sinks and floors, and clear standing water.
**Deny them shelter**: do not stack cardboard against walls, keep stores tidy and keep stock off the floor (on shelves at least 15 to 20 cm up, so you can clean and inspect underneath).
**Keep them out**: fit fly screens and door brushes; keep doors closed; seal gaps around pipes and under doors.
Use first in, first out so no stock sits for months.
Do not feed stray animals at the kitchen door.

blocks.h: If you find signs of pests

ol: Do not touch droppings or dead pests with bare hands.
Tell your supervisor straight away and write what you saw, when and where in the pest log.
Throw away any food or packaging that has been damaged, gnawed or touched by pests. Do not try to use or wash it.
Clean the area with detergent and sanitise the surface (wear gloves).
A licensed pest control contractor should be called to treat the problem. Do not spray insecticide or put out poison yourself in a food area: it can contaminate food and surfaces.

blocks.note: Public health inspectors from the parish health department visit food businesses to check food safety and hygiene, including whether the kitchen is clean, whether staff have Food Handler's Permits and whether there are signs of pests. A clean, signed cleaning schedule and a pest log are the first things they look for.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Hazard
How to prevent harm
rows: Chemicals
Read the label and SDS; wear PPE; never mix; store safely.
Hot water, steam and hot surfaces
Gloves; let things cool; open doors and lids away from the face.
Electric shock
Switch off and unplug before cleaning. Never use water on plugs and sockets or hose down electrical equipment. Check cables.
Sharp blades
Cut-resistant gloves near blades; wash knives one at a time; trained people only for slicers.
Slips
Wet-floor signs; non-slip shoes; wipe up spills; keep hoses and buckets out of walkways.
Lifting and bending
Bend the knees, keep the back straight and the load close. Do not carry a full bucket far; fill it where it will be used, or ask for help.
Fumes
Open windows or use the extractor; never mix products.

ul: Cover or move food and clean equipment before you spray, mop or sweep nearby.
Do not spray chemicals near open food. Spray onto a cloth where you can.
Rinse food-contact surfaces after cleaning if the label says, and wash your hands before you handle food again.

blocks.p: Tell your supervisor about, and write down:

ul: broken, damaged or unsafe equipment (cracked plug, missing guard, leaking fridge);
chemical leaks, spills or missing labels or SDS;
signs of pests, blocked drains or bad smells;
injuries and near misses;
a fridge that is too warm;
cleaning tasks you could not finish and why.

blocks.p: Put an 'out of order' sign on faulty equipment and keep it out of use until it is repaired. Then sign the cleaning schedule for the tasks you have completed.

ul: I can explain the difference between cleaning, disinfecting, sanitising and sterilising.
I can say why a surface is cleaned before it is disinfected or sanitised.
I can list the stages of cleaning a food-contact surface in order.
I can read a label and an SDS and say what each tells me.
I can dilute a cleaning chemical from the label and explain contact time.
I can name the PPE for common cleaning jobs.
I can explain why bleach must never be mixed with acid or ammonia cleaners, and what to do if it happens.
I can store and label chemicals safely, and give first aid for a splash in the eye.
I can describe what a cleaning schedule shows, and why it is signed.
I can clean a bench, a stove, a hood filter, a fryer and a fridge safely.
I can clean a mixer or food processor without putting the motor in water, and say who may clean a slicer.
I can wash up by the three-sink method and use a dishwasher correctly.
I can clean a floor safely with signs, colour-coded equipment and the right order.
I can handle bins, grease traps, used cooking oil and recycling correctly.
I can list the signs of rats, mice, roaches, flies and ants, and say what to do.
I can report faults, hazards and pest signs.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason for each step. For example: 'I scrape and wash the board first, because the sanitiser cannot work through dirt and grease.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: Removing dirt, grease and food waste, usually with detergent and water.
Using a chemical or very hot water to reduce germs on a clean surface.
Reducing germs on a clean surface to a level that is safe for food.
A cleaning product that lifts dirt and grease so that water can carry it away.
A strong detergent for heavy grease.
An acid product that removes lime scale.
A cleaner or pad with fine, gritty particles for scrubbing off burnt-on food.
How long a disinfectant or sanitiser must stay wet on a surface to work.
The maker's sheet on a chemical's dangers, PPE, storage and first aid.
Personal protective equipment, such as gloves and goggles.
The amount of concentrate mixed with water, as the label says.
A written plan of what to clean, how often, how, with what and by whom.
Cleaning spills and tools while you work.
Using different colours of cloths, mops and boards for different areas.
A sink with three bowls: wash, rinse, sanitise.
To let washed items dry on a rack, not with a cloth.
The spread of germs from a dirty item to clean food or surfaces.
A tank on the sink waste pipe that catches fat before it enters the drain.
A rubber-bladed tool for pushing water across a floor.
A full, regular clean in which equipment is moved to clean behind and under it.
A licensed company or person that treats pests.
The rubber strip around a fridge door that keeps the cold in.
Sending used cans, bottles and cardboard to be made into new things.

c1.title: A sharp smell at a villa in Runaway Bay
c1.text: Trainee Shawn has just descaled the dishwasher at a villa in Runaway Bay, using an acid descaler solution in a bucket. The floor is greasy, so he fills the same bucket, which still holds some descaler, with hot water and pours in bleach to mop. A sharp, choking smell rises from the bucket and his eyes sting. The floor cleaner's label says 25 ml of concentrate to 1 litre of water; the proper floor job needs 8 litres of solution.

c2.title: Cleaning the fridge in Ocho Rios
c2.text: Chef Alicia at a hotel in Ocho Rios asks trainee Kemar to clean the reach-in fridge before lunch. It holds raw chicken on the bottom shelf, milk, cut melon and cooked rice, and some of the containers have no label or date. Kemar plans to switch the fridge off and wipe round the food. He also notices black mould in the folds of the door seal.

c3.title: The food processor at a guest house in Mandeville
c3.text: In a guest house kitchen in Mandeville, trainee Tanya is asked to clean the food processor after a busy breakfast. Dried food is caked on the blade and under the lid. She thinks of leaving the whole machine to soak in the sink overnight. Later, after washing the parts, she finds the safety lid does not click into place on the base.

c4.title: Grease build-up at a Negril hotel kitchen
c4.text: At a hotel kitchen in Negril, the cleaning schedule says the cooker hood filters must be washed every week. Chef Orlando sees they have not been signed for five weeks. The filters are dripping with grease, and the deep fryer oil beside them is dark and foams when food goes in.

c5.title: Signs of pests in a Kingston kitchen
c5.text: In a restaurant kitchen in Kingston, Chef Paulette finds small dark droppings behind the dry store shelving, a sack of rice with a chewed corner on the floor, a pile of cardboard boxes against the wall, and a waste bin whose lid is broken. A few cockroaches run out from the floor drain.

c6.title: Washing up after a villa wedding in Treasure Beach
c6.text: After a wedding lunch at a villa in Treasure Beach, trainee Odane has a heap of pots (one with burnt rice), boards and knives. He fills one sink with lukewarm water and a little detergent, puts everything in it, including three knives under the suds, and then dries the pots with a damp tea towel.

questions.q: What is the sharp, choking smell from Shawn's bucket most likely to be?
o: Chlorine gas from bleach reacting with the acid
Steam from the hot water meeting the greasy floor
The normal smell of a strong floor cleaner mixing
Fumes from the dishwasher's hot final rinse water
questions.why: Bleach mixed with an acid such as a descaler gives off chlorine, a poisonous and choking gas. It is not the normal smell of a cleaner, and it can injure the lungs.

questions.q: What should Shawn do first?
o: Stir the bucket well so the two products mix faster
Go into fresh air, warn others and tell his supervisor
Pour the mixture into the kitchen sink and run the tap
Hold his breath and finish mopping the floor quickly
questions.why: Move away from the gas straight away, warn others and report it. Do not try to clear it yourself, because you will breathe more gas. The SDS and the supervisor say how to deal with the spill.

questions.q: How much floor cleaner concentrate does Shawn need to make 8 litres of solution at 25 ml per litre?
o: 25 ml
100 ml
330 ml
200 ml
questions.why: 25 ml × 8 litres = 200 ml. Measure it with a jug or dispenser; a solution that is too weak will not clean well and one that is too strong can harm skin and surfaces.

questions.q: Which habit would best have prevented this accident?
o: Use a clean bucket for each product and never mix products
Always add extra bleach, so the floor is truly clean and safe
Use only very hot water for every cleaning job in the kitchen
Wait until the descaler has dried inside the bucket first
questions.why: Rinsing the bucket and using one product at a time, as the label says, prevents dangerous reactions. Adding more chemical, or relying on hot water, does not make it safer.

questions.q: What should Kemar do with the food before he cleans the fridge?
o: Leave it on a bench for the cleaning time
Wrap it and leave it in the fridge when it is off
Put it all in the freezer to finish cooling
Move it to another fridge or a cool box with ice
questions.why: Food must stay cold while the fridge is cleaned, and benches are in the danger zone. A cool box with ice or another fridge keeps it at 5 °C or below, and gives the chance to check the dates.

questions.q: What should Kemar do with the containers that have no label or date?
o: Throw them away, as their contents cannot be known
Smell each one, and keep those that still smell fresh
Keep them all and write today's date on every label
Reheat them to 74 °C, then put them back in the fridge
questions.why: Food without a label or date cannot be proved safe, and smell is not a reliable test: dangerous bacteria often cause no smell. Unlabelled food is discarded.

questions.q: How should Kemar deal with the mould in the door seal?
o: Cover the mould with a strip of tape so it cannot be seen
Spray strong bleach into the folds, then shut the door at once
Scrub it with a soft brush and detergent, sanitise and dry it
Leave it alone, since the seal is outside the food area
questions.why: Mould in the folds of the seal can spread spores into the fridge and let warm air in. Clean the folds with detergent and a soft brush, sanitise and dry them; report it if the seal is torn.

questions.q: Why is it wrong to leave the whole food processor to soak overnight?
o: The blade will go blunt if it stays in water too long
The plastic parts will soak up the detergent and taint food
The motor base must never go in water: shock and fire risk
The water will go cold and stop the detergent working
questions.why: Only the removable parts go in the sink. Water in the motor base can cause an electric shock or a fire, so the base is wiped with a damp cloth.

questions.q: What is the correct first step before Tanya takes the blade out?
o: Wet the blade first, so the dried food softens up
Put on a cut-resistant glove and pull the blade out
Switch off at the switch and unplug the machine
Run the machine empty to shake the food loose
questions.why: The machine must be impossible to start before you touch a blade. Switch off and unplug, then lift the blade by its handle or hub; never run the machine to clean it.

questions.q: The safety lid will not click into place after cleaning. What should Tanya do?
o: Hold the lid in place with a strong rubber band
Use the machine at the lowest speed setting only
Stop using it, put a sign on it and report it
Use it with the lid off, standing well back from it
questions.why: A guard that does not fit means the safety switch or the lid is damaged. The machine is taken out of use, marked and reported; a makeshift fix could cause an injury.

questions.q: Why are the greasy, overdue filters a danger?
o: Grease in them can catch fire and spread on
They let in too much air, which cools the stove top
They make the fan noisy and slow the hood down a lot
They leave a greasy smell on the food cooked below
questions.why: Grease built up in filters and ducts burns fiercely if a flame or spark reaches it, and a hood fire spreads quickly. Filters must be cleaned on the schedule.

questions.q: How should the filters be cleaned?
o: Wipe the front with a damp cloth while they stay in place
Burn the grease off the mesh with a small blowtorch
Rinse them quickly in cold water, then put them back wet
Lift out when cool, wash with degreaser, rinse, dry, refit
questions.why: Filters are lifted out when the area is cool, washed with a degreaser to cut the grease, rinsed and dried, then refitted the right way round. A cloth wipe leaves the grease in the mesh.

questions.q: What should Chef Orlando do about the missing signatures on the schedule?
o: Find out why, clean now, and record it
Sign for all five weeks, so the chart looks complete
Rub out the line on the chart so nobody asks about it
Do nothing, since the filters will be cleaned next month
questions.why: A schedule shows what was done and by whom. A missed task is reported and cleaned, and the reason is looked into. Signing for work that was not done is dishonest and hides a fire risk.

questions.q: Which of Chef Paulette's findings is most likely to have attracted the pests in the first place?
o: The painted walls behind the dry store shelving
The stainless steel benches standing near the door
The tiled floor around the kitchen drain and gully
The broken bin lid and food left on the floor
questions.why: Pests come for food, water and shelter. Open waste and unsealed food give them an easy meal, and cardboard gives shelter. Fix the lid, store food in sealed containers and off the floor.

questions.q: What should be done with the chewed rice sack?
o: Pour the rice into a new bag and keep on using it
Throw it away, as droppings may be in the rice
Sift out the droppings, then wash the rice well
Use it first, and only in dishes that are cooked well
questions.why: Rats and mice spread germs in their droppings and urine, and these cannot be fully removed from food. Any food touched or chewed by pests is thrown away.

questions.q: Which is the best way to deal with the problem?
o: Spray insecticide freely over the stores, shelves and benches
Put out rat poison on the floor beside the open food
Wait for a few weeks to see whether the signs get worse
Report it, remove food and shelter, call a licensed contractor
questions.why: Report and record the signs, take away what the pests need, and have the infestation treated by a licensed contractor. Sprays and poison used by untrained staff can contaminate food.

questions.q: What is the best way to deal with the pot of burnt rice?
o: Scrape it hard with a knife until the pot is shining clean
Soak it in hot detergent water, then use a suitable scourer
Scour it with steel wool for as long as it takes to shine
Put it away dirty and let the next shift deal with it
questions.why: Soaking in hot detergent softens burnt food so that it lifts with a scourer that will not scratch. Knives and steel wool damage pans, and scratches then trap food and germs.

questions.q: Why is it dangerous to leave knives in the soapy water?
o: The detergent will make the blades go rusty at once
The water will go cold when the metal goes in
Odane may cut his hand on a blade he cannot see
The handles may float to the top and knock the suds off
questions.why: A blade hidden under the suds can cut a hand reaching in. Knives are washed one at a time, handle first, and are put on the rack straight away.

questions.q: Why should Odane change the water part-way through a large wash?
o: Fresh water means less detergent is needed for each load
Cool, greasy water cannot clean or sanitise properly
Clean water makes the knives and pans rust more slowly
A full sink makes the heavy pots too hard to lift out
questions.why: Grease sets and dirt builds up in cool, dirty water, so washing and sanitising fail. Change the water when it is cool, greasy or cloudy.

questions.q: Who may clean a meat slicer?
o: Any kitchen worker, once the slicer has been switched off
A trained person, following the maker's instructions
Whoever used the slicer last, as part of finishing their shift
A trainee, as long as someone else is in the same room
questions.why: A slicer has an extremely sharp blade, so cleaning is limited to trained people who follow the maker's method, switch off, unplug, set the blade gap to zero and wear a cut-resistant glove.
